title: Untrustworthy sources on Facebook and Instagram in 2020: Concentrated exposure but no attitudinal effects
screen_reason: Platform-scale descriptive analysis of all active US adult Facebook and Instagram users (7 August – 23 September 2020) measuring the share of content seen that came from untrustworthy sources (EXPOSURE) and how that exposure is distributed across users and across sources (CONCENTRATION). The accompanying field experiment is an effects study and contributes no prevalence estimates.

estimates.measure_type: % of all content the median active US adult Facebook user saw that came from untrustworthy sources
estimates.value_raw: just 1.1 and 0.1% of the content that the median user saw on Facebook and Instagram, respectively, were from an untrustworthy source
estimates.denominator: All content viewed in Feed by the median US adult monthly active Facebook user (~231 million US accounts accessed Facebook monthly in the second half of 2020)
estimates.definition: Views of original content posted by untrustworthy sources, of content untrustworthy sources reshared, and of content with links to untrustworthy domains
estimates.misinfo_def: "untrustworthy sources … Pages, groups, and domains on Facebook and public accounts on Instagram that had posted or shared two or more pieces of content rated as false or altered media by members of the nonpartisan International Fact-Checking Network"
estimates.n: ~231 million US adult monthly active Facebook accounts
estimates.source_quote: Overall, just 1.1 and 0.1% of the content that the median user saw on Facebook and Instagram, respectively, were from an untrustworthy source.
estimates.page_loc: Results, 'Frequency and sources of exposure to content from untrustworthy sources', p. 4; restated in Discussion, p. 7
estimates.ground_truth_detail: Source-level label built from third-party fact-checker ratings: an entity that had posted or shared two or more pieces of content rated false or altered media by International Fact-Checking Network members partnered with Meta. Meta prioritised content into the fact-checking queue algorithmically and via user reports; the authors note the fact-checking programme's coverage was limited (302 US fact-checks published in January 2020; 180 million pieces of content warning-labelled March–November 2020) and that an Election Integrity Partnership review found only 69% of reported false claims were handled consistently.
estimates.moderator_quote: Our analysis of on-platform exposure and behavior presents aggregated usage levels for the population of US adult Facebook and Instagram users (aged 18 years and over) who accessed Facebook and Instagram at least once in the 30 days preceding 7 August 2020 … During the second half of 2020, 231 million accounts accessed Facebook every month in the US, and 200 million accounts accessed Instagram every month in the US.
estimates.notes: This is a MEDIAN of the user-level distribution, not a mean — the mean would be higher given the heavy right tail. The denominator is all content seen in Feed, not just news or political content, which makes the figure much lower than news-diet-based estimates. Untrustworthy status is a SOURCE-level label (repeat misinformation posters), so exposure includes all content those sources published, not only false content; breadth left blank per the source-level rule. Exposure was measured under Meta's 2020 enforcement regime, which included temporary election-period restrictions; the authors caution the estimates 'may not characterize current levels of exposure' after Meta ended third-party fact-checking in 2025.

estimates.notes: Coded OTHER because the denominator is the composition of a user's FOLLOW GRAPH, not content seen, content published, or content shared — none of the six main constructs fits. It is an exposure-opportunity measure. borderline=true; an adjudicator may prefer to drop it or to recode it CONTENT at source level. The paper gives no count for the denominator. Corresponding medians for Facebook groups and Instagram accounts are zero. Tail values: one Facebook user in 40 followed 12.5% or more untrustworthy Pages or belonged to at least 5.3% untrustworthy groups; one Instagram user in 40 followed 1.9% or more untrustworthy accounts.

missed_or_uncertain: (1) TAIL EXPOSURE SUBGROUPS — not extracted, per the rule to keep the main figure over subgroups, but they are the paper's headline contrast and an adjudicator may want them: content from untrustworthy sources made up 14% of what the top 2.5% of Facebook users saw and 10% of what the top 2.5% of Instagram users saw (~5.8 M and ~5.0 M accounts), i.e. 13x and 103x the median. Reported as '14% or more' / '10% or more' in Results and as flat '14%' / '10%' in the Discussion. (2) CIVIC-CONTENT TAIL FIGURES, also subgroup-and-threshold: for the top 2.5% of Facebook users, 60.9% or more of the civic content seen from Pages and 57.1% or more of that seen from groups came from untrustworthy sources. Striking numbers with a narrower (civic-content) denominator; not extracted for the same reason. (3) COMPOSITION WITHIN UNTRUSTWORTHY EXPOSURE — all denominators are untrustworthy content, so none is a prevalence: untrustworthy Pages = 52.8% of total untrustworthy exposure on Facebook; reshares = 48.3%; only 12.4% of exposures to untrustworthy-Page content was reshared content; on Instagram 68.8% of untrustworthy views were in Home (vs 59.2% of non-untrustworthy views); only 20.5% of untrustworthy exposure came from unconnected accounts. (4) EXPERIMENTAL EXPOSURE LEVELS — not extracted because the experimental sample deliberately oversampled heavy consumers and so is not a population estimate: control-group feed exposure was 1.8% (Facebook Feed) and 2.5% (Instagram Home); control participants saw 5.6 untrustworthy views/day of 243 total on Facebook and 22.9 of 1,050 on Instagram. The treatment cut feed exposure by 73% and 69% (~70%). (5) Table 1's strike and negative-feedback means compare untrustworthy with other sources but are counts per entity, not shares with a denominator. (6) All attitudinal treatment effects are effect estimates, not prevalence. (7) Figures the paper quotes from other studies (20% of Americans -> 62% of untrustworthy-website exposure; 1% of Twitter users -> 70%/80% of exposures) are excluded under R8.

rob.design: Two components. Descriptive: platform-scale observational census of all US adult (18+) monthly active Facebook and Instagram accounts that used the platform at least once in the 30 days before 7 August 2020 (~231 M Facebook, ~200 M Instagram accounts), covering 7 August – 23 September 2020; no sampling, no response rate. Untrustworthy sources identified from third-party fact-checker (IFCN) ratings of two or more pieces of false/altered content; no inter-rater reliability reported, and coverage is bounded by which content fact-checkers were shown. Experimental: preregistered (OSF dt6hz) three-month field experiment, 24 September – 23 December 2020, 15,928 consenting US adults (8,164 Facebook, 7,764 Instagram) recruited by in-feed invitation, block-randomised 50/50, with an oversample of heavy consumers of untrustworthy content; sample skews white, college-educated and Democratic, corrected with post-stratification weights benchmarked to an AmeriSpeak probability sample. Meta-academic collaboration with academic control rights and no prepublication veto. Authors document several data problems: Facebook logging errors restricting the contemporaneous exposure measure to 19–31 October 2020; an Instagram pseudonymisation error that underestimates untrustworthy views by ~8.2%; Instagram carousel logging inconsistencies; retrospective strike totals reconstructed from 2022 data.
rob.item6_quote: we define untrustworthy sources as Pages, groups, and domains on Facebook and public accounts on Instagram that had posted or shared two or more pieces of content rated as false or altered media by members of the nonpartisan International Fact-Checking Network, which independently partnered with Meta to rate content on its platforms in the US until 2025.
rob.item10_quote: Overall, just 1.1 and 0.1% of the content that the median user saw on Facebook and Instagram, respectively, were from an untrustworthy source. … In total, 23% of Facebook users and 11% of Instagram users, representing approximately 53 million and 22 million accounts, respectively, were responsible for 80% of exposure to content from untrustworthy sources on those platforms.
